1.1: From the Heliconian Muses let us begin to sing, who hold the great and holy mount of Helicon, and dance on
1.2: soft feet about the deep-blue spring and the altar of the almighty son of Cronos, and, when they have washed
1.3: their tender bodies in Permessus or in the Horse's Spring or Olmeius, make their fair, lovely dances upon
1.4: highest Helicon and move with vigorous feet. Thence they arise and go abroad by night, veiled in thick mist, and
1.5: utter their song with lovely voice, praising Zeus the aegis-holder and queenly Hera of Argos who walks on golden
1.6: sandals and the daughter of Zeus the aegis-holder bright-eyed Athene, and Phoebus Apollo, and Artemis who
1.7: delights in arrows, and Poseidon the earth-holder who shakes the earth, and reverend Themis and
1.8: quick-glancing  1   Aphrodite, and Hebe with the crown of gold, and fair Dione, Leto,
1.9: Iapetus, and Cronos the crafty counsellor, Eos and great Helius and bright Selene, Earth too, and great Oceanus,
1.10: and dark Night, and the holy race of all the other deathless ones that are for ever. And one day they taught
1.11: Hesiod glorious song while he was shepherding his lambs under holy Helicon, and this word first the goddesses
1.12: said to me – the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who holds the aegis: "Shepherds of the
1.13: wilderness, wretched things of shame, mere bellies, we know how to speak many false things as though they were
1.14: true; but we know, when we will, to utter true things.”
1.15: So said the ready-voiced daughters of great Zeus, and they plucked and gave me a rod, a shoot of sturdy
1.16: laurel, a marvellous thing, and breathed into me a divine voice to celebrate things that shall be and things
1.17: there were aforetime; and they bade me sing of the race of the blessed gods that are eternally, but ever to sing
1.18: of themselves both first and last. But why all this about oak or stone?  2
1.19: Come thou, let us begin with the Muses who gladden the great spirit of their father Zeus in Olympus with
1.20: their songs, telling of things that are and that shall be and that were aforetime with consenting voice.
1.21: Unwearying flows the sweet sound from their lips, and the house of their father Zeus the loud-thunderer is glad
1.22: at the lily-like voice of the goddesses as it spread abroad, and the peaks of snowy Olympus resound, and the
1.23: homes of the immortals. And they uttering their immortal voice, celebrate in song first of all the reverend race
1.24: of the gods from the beginning, those whom Earth and wide Heaven begot, and the gods sprung of these, givers of
1.25: good things. Then, next, the goddesses sing of Zeus, the father of gods and men, as they begin and end their
1.26: strain, how much he is the most excellent among the gods and supreme in power. And again, they chant the race of
1.27: men and strong giants, and gladden the heart of Zeus within Olympus, -- the Olympian Muses, daughters of Zeus
1.29: Them in Pieria did Mnemosyne (Memory), who reigns over the hills of Eleuther, bear of union with the
1.30: father, the son of Cronos, a forgetting of ills and a rest from sorrow. For nine nights did wise Zeus lie with
1.31: her, entering her holy bed remote from the immortals. And when a year was passed and the seasons came round as
1.32: the months waned, and many days were accomplished, she bare nine daughters, all of one mind, whose hearts are
1.33: set upon song and their spirit free from care, a little way from the topmost peak of snowy Olympus. There are
1.34: their bright dancing-places and beautiful homes, and beside them the Graces and Himerus (Desire) live in
1.35: delight. And they, uttering through their lips a lovely voice, sing the laws of all and the goodly ways of the
1.36: immortals, uttering their lovely voice. Then went they to Olympus, delighting in their sweet voice, with
1.37: heavenly song, and the dark earth resounded about them as they chanted, and a lovely sound rose up beneath their
1.38: feet as they went to their father. And he was reigning in heaven, himself holding the lightning and glowing
1.39: thunderbolt, when he had overcome by might his father Cronos; and he distributed fairly to the immortals their
1.41: These things, then, the Muses sang who dwell on Olympus, nine daughters begotten by great Zeus, Cleio and
1.42: Euterpe, Thaleia, Melpomene and Terpsichore, and Erato and Polyhymnia and Urania and Calliope,  3   who is the chiefest of them all, for she attends on worshipful princes: whomsoever of
1.43: heaven-nourished princes the daughters of great Zeus honour, and behold him at his birth, they pour sweet dew
1.44: upon his tongue, and from his lips flow gracious words. All the people look towards him while he settles causes
1.45: with true judgements: and he, speaking surely, would soon make wise end even of a great quarrel; for therefore
1.46: are there princes wise in heart, because when the people are being misguided in their assembly, they set right
1.47: the matter again with ease, persuading them with gentle words. And when he passes through a gathering, they
1.48: greet him as a god with gentle reverence, and he is conspicuous amongst the assembled: such is the holy gift of
1.49: the Muses to men. For it is through the Muses and far-shooting Apollo that there are singers and harpers upon
1.50: the earth; but princes are of Zeus, and happy is he whom the Muses love: sweet flows speech from his mouth. For
1.51: though a man have sorrow and grief in his newly-troubled soul and live in dread because his heart is distressed,
1.52: yet, when a singer, the servant of the Muses, chants the glorious deeds of men of old and the blessed gods who
1.53: inhabit Olympus, at once he forgets his heaviness and remembers not his sorrows at all; but the gifts of the
1.54: goddesses soon turn him away from these.
1.55: Hail, children of Zeus! Grant lovely song and celebrate the holy race of the deathless gods who are for
1.56: ever, those that were born of Earth and starry Heaven and gloomy Night and them that briny Sea did rear. Tell
1.57: how at the first gods and earth came to be, and rivers, and the boundless sea with its raging swell, and the
1.58: gleaming stars, and the wide heaven above, and the gods who were born of them, givers of good things, and how
1.59: they divided their wealth, and how they shared their honours amongst them, and also how at the first they took
1.60: many-folded Olympus. These things declare to me from the beginning, ye Muses who dwell in the house of Olympus,
1.61: and tell me which of them first came to be.

2.1: Verily at the first Chaos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Earth, the ever-sure foundations of
2.2: all  4   the deathless ones who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and dim Tartarus in
2.3: the depth of the wide-pathed Earth, and Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs
2.4: and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them. From Chaos came forth Erebus and
2.5: black Night; but of Night were born Aether  5   and Day, whom she conceived and bare
2.6: from union in love with Erebus. And Earth first bare starry Heaven, equal to herself, to cover her on every
2.7: side, and to be an ever-sure abiding-place for the blessed gods. And she brought forth long Hills, graceful
2.8: haunts of the goddess-Nymphs who dwell amongst the glens of the hills. She bare also the fruitless deep with his
2.9: raging swell, Pontus, without sweet union of love.

3.1: But afterwards she lay with Heaven and bare deep-swirling Oceanus, Coeus and Crius and Hyperion and
3.2: Iapetus, Theia and Rhea, Themis and Mnemosyne and gold-crowned Phoebe and lovely Tethys. After them was born
3.3: Cronos the wily, youngest and most terrible of her children, and he hated his lusty sire.
3.4: And again, she bare the Cyclopes, overbearing in spirit, Brontes, and Steropes and stubborn-hearted
3.5: Arges,  6   who gave Zeus the thunder and made the thunderbolt: in all else they were
3.6: like the gods, but one eye only was set in the midst of their fore-heads. And they were surnamed Cyclopes
3.7: (Orb-eyed) because one orbed eye was set in their foreheads. Strength and might and craft were in their works.
3.8: And again, three other sons were born of Earth and Heaven, great and doughty beyond telling, Cottus and
3.9: Briareos and Gyes, presumptuous children. From their shoulders sprang an hundred arms, not to be approached, and
3.10: each had fifty heads upon his shoulders on their strong limbs, and irresistible was the stubborn strength that
3.11: was in their great forms. For of all the children that were born of Earth and Heaven, these were the most
3.12: terrible, and they were hated by their own father from the first. And he used to hide them all away in a secret
3.13: place of Earth so soon as each was born, and would not suffer them to come up into the light: and Heaven
3.14: rejoiced in his evil doing. But vast Earth groaned within, being straitened, and she made the element of grey
3.15: flint and shaped a great sickle, and told her plan to her dear sons.
3.16: And she spoke, cheering them, while she was vexed in her dear heart: “My children, gotten of a
3.17: sinful father, if you will obey me, we should punish the vile outrage of your father; for he first thought of
3.19: So she said; but fear seized them all, and none of them uttered a word. But great Cronos the wily took
3.20: courage and answered his dear mother: “Mother, I will undertake to do this deed, for I reverence not our
3.21: father of evil name, for he first thought of doing shameful things.”
3.22: So he said: and vast Earth rejoiced greatly in spirit, and set and hid him in an ambush, and put in his
3.23: hands a jagged sickle, and revealed to him the whole plot.
3.24: And Heaven came, bringing on night and longing for love, and he lay about Earth spreading himself full
3.25: upon her.  7   Then the son from his ambush stretched forth his left hand and in his
3.26: right took the great long sickle with jagged teeth, and swiftly lopped off his own father's members and cast
3.27: them away to fall behind him. And not vainly did they fall from his hand; for all the bloody drops that gushed
3.28: forth Earth received, and as the seasons moved round she bare the strong Erinyes and the great Giants with
3.29: gleaming armour, holding long spears in their hands and the Nymphs whom they call Meliae  8   all over the boundless earth. And so soon as he had cut off the members with flint
3.30: and cast them from the land into the surging sea, they were swept away over the main a long time: and a white
3.31: foam spread around them from the immortal flesh, and in it there grew a maiden. First she drew near holy
3.32: Cythera, and from there, afterwards, she came to sea-girt Cyprus, and came forth an awful and lovely goddess,
3.33: and grass grew up about her beneath her shapely feet. Her gods and men call Aphrodite, and the foam-born goddess
3.34: and rich-crowned Cytherea, because she grew amid the foam, and Cytherea because she reached Cythera, and
3.35: Cyprogenes because she was born in billowy Cyprus, and Philommedes  9   because sprang
3.36: from the members. And with her went Eros, and comely Desire followed her at her birth at the first and as she
3.37: went into the assembly of the gods. This honour she has from the beginning, and this is the portion allotted to
3.38: her amongst men and undying gods, -- the whisperings of maidens and smiles and deceits with sweet delight and
3.40: But these sons whom be begot himself great Heaven used to call Titans (Strainers) in reproach, for he
3.41: said that they strained and did presumptuously a fearful deed, and that vengeance for it would come afterwards.

4.1: And Night bare hateful Doom and black Fate and Death, and she bare Sleep and the tribe of Dreams. And
4.2: again the goddess murky Night, though she lay with none, bare Blame and painful Woe, and the Hesperides who
4.3: guard the rich, golden apples and the trees bearing fruit beyond glorious Ocean. Also she bare the Destinies and
4.4: ruthless avenging Fates, Clotho and Lachesis and Atropos,  10   who give men at their
4.5: birth both evil and good to have, and they pursue the transgressions of men and of gods: and these goddesses
4.6: never cease from their dread anger until they punish the sinner with a sore penalty. Also deadly Night bare
4.7: Nemesis (Indignation) to afflict mortal men, and after her, Deceit and Friendship and hateful Age and
4.9: But abhorred Strife bare painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings also,
4.10: Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin, all of one nature, and
4.11: Oath who most troubles men upon earth when anyone wilfully swears a false oath.

5.1: And Sea begat Nereus, the eldest of his children, who is true and lies not: and men call him the Old Man
5.2: because he is trusty and gentle and does not forget the laws of righteousness, but thinks just and kindly
5.3: thoughts. And yet again he got great Thaumas and proud Phoreys, being mated with Earth, and fair-cheeked Ceto
5.4: and Eurybia who has a heart of flint within her.
5.5: And of Nereus and rich-haired Doris, daughter of Ocean the perfect river, were born children,  11   passing lovely amongst goddesses, Ploto, Eucrante, Sao, and Amphitrite, and Eudora,
5.6: and Thetis, Galene and Glauce, Cymothoe, Speo, Thoe and lovely Halie, and Pasithea, and Erato, and rosy-armed
5.7: Eunice, and gracious Melite, and Eulimene, and Agaue, Doto, Proto, Pherusa, and Dynamene, and Nisaea, and
5.8: Actaea, and Protomedea, Doris, Panopea, and comely Galatea, and lovely Hippothoe, and rosy-armed Hipponoe, and
5.9: Cymodoce who with Cymatolege  12   and Amphitrite easily calms the waves upon the
5.10: misty sea and the blasts of raging winds, and Cymo, and Eione, and rich-crowned Alimede, and Glauconome, fond of
5.11: laughter, and Pontoporea, Leagore, Euagore, and Laomedea, and Polynoe, and Autonoe, and Lysianassa, and Euarne,
5.12: lovely of shape and without blemish of form, and Psamathe of charming figure and divine Menippe, Neso, Eupompe,
5.13: Themisto, Pronoe, and Nemertes  13   who has the nature of her deathless father. These
5.14: fifty daughters sprang from blameless Nereus, skilled in excellent crafts.
5.15: And Thaumas wedded Electra the daughter of deep-flowing Ocean, and she bare him swift Iris and the
5.16: long-haired Harpies, Aello (Storm-swift) and Ocypetes (Swift-flier) who on their swift wings keep pace with the
5.17: blasts of the winds and the birds; for quick as time they dart along.

6.1: And again, Ceto bare to Phorcys the fair-cheeked Graiae, sisters grey from their birth: and both
6.2: deathless gods and men who walk on earth call them Graiae, Pemphredo well-clad, and saffron-robed Enyo, and the
6.3: Gorgons who dwell beyond glorious Ocean in the frontier land towards Night where are the clear-voiced
6.4: Hesperides, Sthenno, and Euryale, and Medusa who suffered a woeful fate: she was mortal, but the two were
6.5: undying and grew not old. With her lay the Dark-haired One  14   in a soft meadow amid
6.6: spring flowers. And when Perseus cut off her head, there sprang forth great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus who
6.7: is so called because he was born near the springs ( pegae ) of Ocean; and that other, because he held a
6.8: golden blade ( aor ) in his hands. Now Pegasus flew away and left the earth, the mother of flocks, and
6.9: came to the deathless gods: and he dwells in the house of Zeus and brings to wise Zeus the thunder and
6.10: lightning. But Chrysaor was joined in love to Callirrhoe, the daughter of glorious Ocean, and begot three-headed
6.11: Geryones. Him mighty Heracles slew in sea-girt Erythea by his shambling oxen on that day when he drove the
6.12: wide-browed oxen to holy Tiryns, and had crossed the ford of Ocean and killed Orthus and Eurytion the herdsman
6.13: in the dim stead out beyond glorious Ocean.
6.14: And in a hollow cave she bare another monster, irresistible, in no wise like either to mortal men or to
6.15: the undying gods, even the goddess fierce Echidna who is half a nymph with glancing eyes and fair cheeks, and
6.16: half again a huge snake, great and awful, with speckled skin, eating raw flesh beneath the secret parts of the
6.17: holy earth. And there she has a cave deep down under a hollow rock far from the deathless gods and mortal men.
6.18: There, then, did the gods appoint her a glorious house to dwell in: and she keeps guard in Arima beneath the
6.19: earth, grim Echidna, a nymph who dies not nor grows old all her days.
6.20: Men say that Typhaon the terrible, outrageous and lawless, was joined in love to her, the maid with
6.21: glancing eyes. So she conceived and brought forth fierce offspring; first she bare Orthus the hound of Geryones,
6.22: and then again she bare a second, a monster not to be overcome and that may not be described, Cerberus who eats
6.23: raw flesh, the brazen-voiced hound of Hades, fifty-headed, relentless and strong. And again she bore a third,
6.24: the evil-minded Hydra of Lerna, whom the goddess, white-armed Hera nourished, being angry beyond measure with
6.25: the mighty Heracles. And her Heracles, the son of Zeus, of the house of Amphitryon, together with warlike
6.26: Iolaus, destroyed with the unpitying sword through the plans of Athene the spoil-driver. She was the mother of
6.27: Chimaera who breathed raging fire, a creature fearful, great, swift-footed and strong, who had three heads, one
6.28: of a grim-eyed lion; in her hinderpart, a dragon; and in her middle, a goat, breathing forth a fearful blast of
6.29: blazing fire. Her did Pegasus and noble Bellerophon slay; but Echidna was subject in love to Orthus and brought
6.30: forth the deadly Sphinx which destroyed the Cadmeans, and the Nemean lion, which Hera, the good wife of Zeus,
6.31: brought up and made to haunt the hills of Nemea, a plague to men. There he preyed upon the tribes of her own
6.32: people and had power over Tretus of Nemea and Apesas: yet the strength of stout Heracles overcame him.
6.33: And Ceto was joined in love to Phorcys and bare her youngest, the awful snake who guards the apples all
6.34: of gold in the secret places of the dark earth at its great bounds. This is the offspring of Ceto and Phorcys.

7.1: And Tethys bare to Ocean eddying rivers, Nilus, and Alpheus, and deep-swirling Eridanus, Strymon, and
7.2: Meander, and the fair stream of Ister, and Phasis, and Rhesus, and the silver eddies of Achelous, Nessus, and
7.3: Rhodius, Haliacmon, and Heptaporus, Granicus, and Aesepus, and holy Simois, and Peneus, and Hermus, and Caicus
7.4: fair stream, and great Sangarius, Ladon, Parthenius, Euenus, Ardescus, and divine Scamander.
7.5: Also she brought forth a holy company of daughters  15   who with the lord
7.6: Apollo and the Rivers have youths in their keeping -- to this charge Zeus appointed them -- Peitho, and Admete,
7.7: and Ianthe, and Electra, and Doris, and Prymno, and Urania divine in form, Hippo, Clymene, Rhodea, and
7.8: Callirrhoe, Zeuxo and Clytie, and Idyia, and Pasithoe, Plexaura, and Galaxaura, and lovely Dione, Melobosis and
7.9: Thoe and handsome Polydora, Cerceis lovely of form, and soft eyed Pluto, Perseis, Ianeira, Acaste, Xanthe,
7.10: Petraea the fair, Menestho, and Europa, Metis, and Eurynome, and Telesto saffron-clad, Chryseis and Asia and
7.11: charming Calypso, Eudora, and Tyche, Amphirho, and Ocyrrhoe, and Styx who is the chiefest of them all. These are
7.12: the eldest daughters that sprang from Ocean and Tethys; but there are many besides. For there are three thousand
7.13: neat-ankled daughters of Ocean who are dispersed far and wide, and in every place alike serve the earth and the
7.14: deep waters, children who are glorious among goddesses. And as many other rivers are there, babbling as they
7.15: flow, sons of Ocean, whom queenly Tethys bare, but their names it is hard for a mortal man to tell, but people
7.16: know those by which they severally dwell.
7.17: And Theia was subject in love to Hyperion and bare great Helius (Sun) and clear Selene (Moon) and Eos
7.18: (Dawn) who shines upon all that are on earth and upon the deathless Gods who live in the wide heaven.
7.19: And Eurybia, bright goddess, was joined in love to Crius and bare great Astraeus, and Pallas, and Perses
7.20: who also was eminent among all men in wisdom.
7.21: And Eos bare to Astraeus the strong-hearted winds, brightening Zephyrus, and Boreas, headlong in his
7.22: course, and Notus, -- a goddess mating in love with a god. And after these Erigenia  16   bare the star Eosphorus (Dawn-bringer), and the gleaming stars with which heaven is
7.24: And Styx the daughter of Ocean was joined to Pallas and bare Zelus (Emulation) and trim-ankled Nike
7.25: (Victory) in the house. Also she brought forth Cratos (Strength) and Bia (Force), wonderful children. These have
7.26: no house apart from Zeus, nor any dwelling nor path except that wherein God leads them, but they dwell always
7.27: with Zeus the loud-thunderer. For so did Styx the deathless daughter of Ocean plan on that day when the Olympian
7.28: Lightener called all the deathless gods to great Olympus, and said that whosoever of the gods would fight with
7.29: him against the Titans, he would not cast him out from his rights, but each should have the office which he had
7.30: before amongst the deathless gods. And he declared that he who was without office and rights as is just. So
7.31: deathless Styx came first to Olympus with her children through the wit of her dear father. And Zeus honoured
7.32: her, and gave her very great gifts, for her he appointed to be the great oath of the gods, and her children to
7.33: live with him always. And as he promised, so he performed fully unto them all. But he himself mightily reigns
7.35: Again, Phoebe came to the desired embrace of Coeus. Then the goddess through the love of the god
7.36: conceived and brought forth dark-gowned Leto, always mild, kind to men and to the deathless gods, mild from the
7.37: beginning, gentlest in all Olympus. Also she bare Asteria of happy name, whom Perses once led to his great house
7.38: to be called his dear wife.

8.1: And she conceived and bare Hecate whom Zeus the son of Cronos honoured above all. He gave her splendid
8.2: gifts, to have a share of the earth and the unfruitful sea. She received honour also in starry heaven, and is
8.3: honoured exceedingly by the deathless gods. For to this day, whenever any one of men on earth offers rich
8.4: sacrifices and prays for favour according to custom, he calls upon Hecate. Great honour comes full easily to him
8.5: whose prayers the goddess receives favourably, and she bestows wealth upon him; for the power surely is with
8.6: her. For as many as were born of Earth and Ocean amongst all these she has her due portion. The son of Cronos
8.7: did her no wrong nor took anything away of all that was her portion among the former Titan gods: but she holds,
8.8: as the division was at the first from the beginning, privilege both in earth, and in heaven, and in sea. Also,
8.9: because she is an only child, the goddess receives not less honour, but much more still, for Zeus honours her.
8.10: Whom she will she greatly aids and advances: she sits by worshipful kings in judgement, and in the assembly whom
8.11: she will is distinguished among the people. And when men arm themselves for the battle that destroys men, then
8.12: the goddess is at hand to give victory and grant glory readily to whom she will. Good is she also when men
8.13: contend at the games, for there too the goddess is with them and profits them: and he who by might and strength
8.14: gets the victory wins the rich prize easily with joy, and brings glory to his parents. And she is good to stand
8.15: by horsemen, whom she will: and to those whose business is in the grey discomfortable sea, and who pray to
8.16: Hecate and the loud-crashing Earth-Shaker, easily the glorious goddess gives great catch, and easily she takes
8.17: it away as soon as seen, if so she will. She is good in the byre with Hermes to increase the stock. The droves
8.18: of kine and wide herds of goats and flocks of fleecy sheep, if she will, she increases from a few, or makes many
8.19: to be less. So, then. albeit her mother's only child,  17   she is honoured amongst
8.20: all the deathless gods. And the son of Cronos made her a nurse of the young who after that day saw with their
8.21: eyes the light of all-seeing Dawn. So from the beginning she is a nurse of the young, and these are her honours.

9.1: But Rhea was subject in love to Cronos and bare splendid children, Hestia,  18   Demeter, and gold-shod Hera and strong Hades, pitiless in heart, who dwells under
9.2: the earth, and the loud-crashing Earth-Shaker, and wise Zeus, father of gods and men, by whose thunder the wide
9.3: earth is shaken. These great Cronos swallowed as each came forth from the womb to his mother's knees with this
9.4: intent, that no other of the proud sons of Heaven should hold the kingly office amongst the deathless gods. For
9.5: he learned from Earth and starry Heaven that he was destined to be overcome by his own son, strong though he
9.6: was, through the contriving of great Zeus.  19   Therefore he kept no blind outlook,
9.7: but watched and swallowed down his children: and unceasing grief seized Rhea. But when she was about to bear
9.8: Zeus, the father of gods and men, then she besought her own dear parents, Earth and starry Heaven, to devise
9.9: some plan with her that the birth of her dear child might be concealed, and that retribution might overtake
9.10: great, crafty Cronos for his own father and also for the children whom he had swallowed down. And they readily
9.11: heard and obeyed their dear daughter, and told her all that was destined to happen touching Cronos the king and
9.12: his stout-hearted son. So they sent her to Lyetus, to the rich land of Crete, when she was ready to bear great
9.13: Zeus, the youngest of her children. Him did vast Earth receive from Rhea in wide Crete to nourish and to bring
9.14: up. Thither came Earth carrying him swiftly through the black night to Lyctus first, and took him in her arms
9.15: and hid him in a remote cave beneath the secret places of the holy earth on thick-wooded Mount Aegeum; but to
9.16: the mightily ruling son of Heaven, the earlier king of the gods, she gave a great stone wrapped in swaddling
9.17: clothes. Then he took it in his hands and thrust it down into his belly: wretch! he knew not in his heart that
9.18: in place of the stone his son was left behind, unconquered and untroubled, and that he was soon to overcome him
9.19: by force and might and drive him from his honours, himself to reign over the deathless gods.
9.20: After that, the strength and glorious limbs of the prince increased quickly, and as the years rolled on,
9.21: great Cronos the wily was beguiled by the deep suggestions of Earth, and brought up again his offspring,
9.22: vanquished by the arts and might of his own son, and he vomited up first the stone which he had swallowed last.
9.23: And Zeus set it fast in the wide-pathed earth at goodly Pytho under the glens of Parnassus, to be a sign
9.24: thenceforth and a marvel to mortal men.  20   And he set free from their deadly bonds
9.25: the brothers of his father, sons of Heaven whom his father in his foolishness had bound. And they remembered to
9.26: be grateful to him for his kindness, and gave him thunder and the glowing thunderbolt and lightening: for before
9.27: that, huge Earth had hidden these. In them he trusts and rules over mortals and immortals.

10.1: Now Iapetus took to wife the neat-ankled mad Clymene, daughter of Ocean, and went up with her into one
10.2: bed. And she bare him a stout-hearted son, Atlas: also she bare very glorious Menoetius and clever Prometheus,
